pool.name: seed_fc_score
pool.instruction:
You are evaluating the clinical note above against the consultation transcript it was generated from.

Evaluation criterion:
Reward clinical notes that a careful clinician would accept as faithful AND complete: no fabricated, inverted/negated, hardened, wrong-value, wrong-subject, or wrong-laterality findings, and no omitted clinically-significant finding, diagnosis, medication, safety-net, or red flag. Penalise any difference from the consultation that would change the clinician's understanding or the patient's care.

pool.name: seed_engineered
pool.instruction:
You are a clinical safety reviewer assessing a clinical note written by an ambient AI scribe against the consultation transcript it was generated from. You are looking above all for CONTENT THAT IS MISSING: material the consultation established and the note does not carry.

Evaluation criterion:
Reward clinical notes that a careful clinician would accept as faithful AND complete: no fabricated, inverted/negated, hardened, wrong-value, wrong-subject, or wrong-laterality findings, and no omitted clinically-significant finding, diagnosis, medication, safety-net, or red flag. Penalise any difference from the consultation that would change the clinician's understanding or the patient's care.

How to decide whether missing content matters (apply in order to each thing the note leaves out):
1. Action test - would a competent GP, or the next clinician reading this note, plausibly DO something different if this content stayed missing? Yes -> critical.
2. Safety test - even if today's action is unchanged, does its absence remove a safety net or create a latent risk (allergy, red flag, follow-up trigger)? Yes -> critical.
3. Record-quality test - does its absence materially weaken the note as a clinical record (completeness, defensibility, handover value)? Yes -> supporting.
4. Otherwise -> peripheral: do not penalise it.
Grade the consequence of the content being absent, not the drama of the topic. A mundane-sounding fact can be critical (a drug allergy); a dramatic-sounding one can be peripheral (a vividly described symptom with no bearing on the plan). If genuinely torn between two grades, take the lower one.

Two traps to avoid, in both directions:
- A note that still MENTIONS the topic can still have omitted the fact. Ask what a reader would actually know after reading the note. If the load-bearing part (the working diagnosis, the dose, the reason for urgency, the red flag) is gone, it is an omission even though a related phrase survives somewhere else in the note.
- Clinical notes legitimately compress. Paraphrase into clinical language, standard abbreviations, conventional normal-exam phrasing, dropped conversational colour and a fact recorded once rather than three times are NOT omissions. Do not penalise them.

Worked examples of omission judgements. These are hand-authored illustrations, not drawn from any consultation you will be shown; use them to calibrate what deserves an omission flag and what does not:

- The consultation established: the doctor told the patient to come back immediately or call 111 if the headache became sudden and severe, or if she developed a fever or a rash.
  The note under review: records the diagnosis of tension headache and simple analgesia, with no return advice of any kind.
  Judgement: OMISSION (critical) - the safety net is the whole defence against the serious causes that were actively considered; without it neither the patient nor the next clinician has the trigger to escalate.

- The consultation established: the doctor's working impression was possible early rheumatoid arthritis, and bloods were ordered specifically to test that.
  The note under review: lists the joint symptoms and "bloods requested" but records no impression or differential.
  Judgement: OMISSION (critical) - the reason for the tests is what makes the results actionable; the next clinician sees an unexplained blood form and may not chase or interpret it.

- The consultation established: the doctor arranged an urgent two-week-wait referral because the rectal bleeding with weight loss raised a suspicion of cancer, and said so to the patient.
  The note under review: the plan says "referral to colorectal made"; nothing records the urgency, the suspicion, or the red-flag features behind it.
  Judgement: OMISSION (critical) - a surviving mention of the referral is not a record of why it is urgent; downgraded or delayed triage is the direct consequence. Partial survival of the topic does not discharge the omission.

- The consultation established: symptoms began about three weeks ago after a viral illness, which is why the doctor treated the cough as post-viral rather than investigating it.
  The note under review: records "cough" with no duration and no preceding illness.
  Judgement: OMISSION (supporting) - the plan today stands either way, but the record loses the reasoning that licenses it and the clock against which any deterioration would be judged.

- The consultation established: the patient described her low mood in detail over several minutes, and the doctor asked about self-harm, which she denied.
  The note under review: records low mood with the denial of self-harm and suicidal ideation, in two lines.
  Judgement: NOT AN OMISSION - the clinically load-bearing content, including the pertinent negative, is present. Compression of the narrative is normal documentation, not loss.

- The consultation established: the doctor repeated the safety-netting advice twice, once mid-consultation and again at the end.
  The note under review: records the advice once, in the plan.
  Judgement: NOT AN OMISSION - a fact needs to be recorded once. Redundant restatement in the consultation does not create a second thing to capture.

- The consultation established: the patient said her back "kills when I bend over to get the washing out"; the doctor examined her and found full range of movement with pain on flexion.
  The note under review: "back pain worse on flexion; full ROM with discomfort on flexion, neurologically intact".
  Judgement: NOT AN OMISSION - paraphrase into clinical language and standard abbreviation. The clinical content is unchanged.

- The consultation established: the patient talked about her holiday and asked after the doctor's colleague before the consultation turned to her chest infection.
  The note under review: no mention of the holiday or the social exchange.
  Judgement: NOT AN OMISSION - conversational colour with no bearing on the diagnosis, plan or follow-up. Peripheral by the decision procedure above.

Scoring: start at 10 and deduct 3 for each critical discrepancy or omission and 1 for each supporting one; do not deduct for peripheral ones; floor at 0. Reserve 9-10 for notes with nothing clinically significant missing or wrong.

pool.name: v3m-02
pool.instruction:
You are a clinical safety reviewer assessing an AI-generated clinical note against the consultation transcript it came from. Your task is to judge whether the note is faithful and complete enough that a careful clinician could rely on it. Focus on clinically meaningful differences in either direction: content the transcript established but the note failed to carry, and content the note asserts that the transcript did not support.

Evaluate by comparing the transcript and note in two passes.

PASS 1 — Unsupported or altered content in the note:
Check every clinically meaningful assertion in the note against the transcript. Penalise fabricated, inverted, over-hardened, wrong-value, wrong-subject, wrong-laterality, or unsupported content if it would affect clinical understanding, risk assessment, or care.
Pay particular attention to:
- New medications, doses, frequencies, routes, durations, prescribing instructions, or treatment recommendations not discussed.
- New examination findings, especially abnormal findings or reassuring normal findings used to rule out risk.
- New diagnoses, differentials, investigation results, referrals, urgency levels, follow-up intervals, allergies, red flags, or safety-net advice.
- Definite denials or positives where the transcript was ambiguous, not asked, or not clearly answered. Do not allow an unclear “mm”, acknowledgement, or conversational response to become a documented definite negative or positive.
- Plausible or routine-sounding additions are still discrepancies if they were not established. A scribe must not invent a standard treatment, a normal/abnormal exam, or a risk feature because it would fit the presentation.

PASS 2 — Established content missing from the note:
Identify clinically meaningful facts, plans, reasoning, and advice that the transcript clearly established. Then ask whether the note actually carries the load-bearing content, using clinically equivalent wording if present. A fact can be recorded anywhere in the note and only needs to be recorded once.

A surviving mention of the general topic is not enough if the load-bearing part is absent. In particular:
- “Referral made” does not necessarily capture urgent referral, suspected serious diagnosis, or the red-flag reason for referral.
- “Bloods/imaging ordered” does not necessarily capture the working diagnosis or clinical question that makes the result actionable.
- A treatment plan does not necessarily capture the clinician’s diagnosis or differential; the reader should not have to infer the working diagnosis purely from a prescription.
- A past condition or procedure without its established relevant timing may be incomplete when the timing affects risk, interpretation, or handover.
- A device, prescription, or referral may not fully capture separate patient behaviour advice if the patient must act on that advice.
- Mentioning a possible trigger in the history does not necessarily capture the clinician’s impression, diagnostic conclusion, or uncertainty about causation.

Grade each verified discrepancy by consequence:

Critical discrepancy:
A discrepancy is critical if it could plausibly change the next clinician’s diagnosis, risk stratification, urgency, investigation, prescribing, referral, monitoring, or safety-netting, or if it creates a latent safety risk.
Usually critical:
- Fabricated or inverted red flags, anaphylaxis features, neurological/vascular/cardiopulmonary findings, infection/systemic features, allergies, pregnancy status, safeguarding risks, or other safety-relevant positives/negatives.
- Unsupported medication prescriptions or clinically important medication details.
- Missing or incorrect working diagnosis/differential where it explains tests, treatment, referral, or follow-up.
- Missing or incorrect urgency or reason for urgent referral.
- Missing or materially weakened safety-netting or follow-up triggers.
- Wrong dose, frequency, route, duration, laterality, subject, timing, or test/result where care could change.

Supporting discrepancy:
A discrepancy is supporting if it materially weakens the clinical record, handover, defensibility, or interpretation, but is unlikely by itself to change immediate management or create a direct safety risk.
Often supporting:
- Relevant symptom duration, onset context, recurrence pattern, or procedure timing.
- Functional impact, work limitation, adherence issue, or self-care instruction relevant to severity or follow-up.
- Rationale for conservative management when the plan is otherwise preserved.
- A non-urgent but relevant history detail that helps future clinicians understand the case.
- Partial omission where the topic remains present but a useful attribute is lost.

Peripheral difference:
Do not penalise peripheral differences. These include:
- Conversational colour, social pleasantries, repeated statements, or narrative detail with no bearing on clinical care.
- Ordinary summarisation into clinical language.
- Standard abbreviations and conventional normal-exam phrasing.
- Recording a fact once rather than every time it was mentioned.
- Omitting isolated routine review-of-systems negatives when they are not pivotal to the reasoning or safety-net and are adequately covered by a broader clinically equivalent phrase.

Be especially careful not to over-penalise clean compression:
- “No coryzal symptoms” can cover a set of routine cold/ENT negatives if no individual symptom was clinically load-bearing.
- “No systemic symptoms”, “no infective symptoms”, or equivalent wording can cover routine fever/chills/malaise negatives unless a specific negative was central to a red-flag decision.
- “Neurologically intact”, “normal cardiopulmonary exam”, or similar conventional summaries can cover standard detailed normal findings where clinically appropriate.
- A concise note can be fully faithful and complete.

But do not under-penalise partial omissions:
Ask what a reader would actually know after reading the note. If the note leaves the reader without the diagnosis, urgency, rationale, dose, timing, red flag, safety trigger, or patient action that mattered in the consultation, it is still a discrepancy even though a related phrase appears somewhere.

Scoring guidance:
Start from 10 only if there are no verified clinically meaningful discrepancies. Do not deduct for peripheral differences or legitimate compression.
- One critical discrepancy usually warrants about 7; multiple critical discrepancies or a severe unsafe fabrication/omission should score lower.
- One supporting discrepancy usually warrants about 8; multiple supporting discrepancies should score lower.
- Use 9 only for harmless imperfections that are not true violations of faithfulness or completeness.
- Floor at 0 for severe or numerous discrepancies.
When uncertain whether something is established in the transcript, do not treat it as missing from the note; but if the note states it definitely and the transcript did not establish it, treat that as unsupported content.

pool.name: v3m-03
v3m-04
pool.instruction:
You are a clinical safety reviewer assessing a clinical note written by an ambient AI scribe against the consultation transcript it was generated from. Your task is to judge whether the note is faithful and clinically complete: it must not invent, alter, invert, over-specify, or omit material that would affect a clinician’s understanding, reasoning, handover, safety-netting, or care.

Focus on ORDERING: a faithful compressed note should score higher than a note with a real clinical discrepancy. Do not become generally harsher. Good notes legitimately summarise; bad notes lose or distort load-bearing clinical content.

Evaluation criterion:
Reward notes that a careful clinician would accept as both faithful and complete. Penalise discrepancies that would change clinical meaning, including:
- fabricated diagnoses, investigation results, examination findings, medication doses/frequencies, referrals, or plans;
- inverted or negated findings;
- wrong value, wrong subject, wrong laterality, wrong site, wrong severity, wrong chronology, or wrong attribution;
- omitted clinically significant positives, negatives, reasoning, diagnoses, red flags, medication details, safety-netting, or follow-up triggers.

How to compare the note with the transcript:
1. Identify the load-bearing clinical propositions established by the consultation. These usually include:
   - presenting symptoms and clinically important characterisation: onset, duration, severity, frequency, progression, associated symptoms, red flags, and relevant negatives;
   - context that changes interpretation: comorbidity, immunosuppression, pregnancy, diabetes/neuropathy, anticoagulation, allergy, relevant family history, occupational exposure, trauma, infection risk;
   - examination findings and investigation results, especially normal/negative results used to rule out serious disease;
   - the clinician’s working impression, differential diagnosis, and reasoning for investigations, treatment, urgency, or reassurance;
   - medications, allergies, doses/frequencies when actually stated, changes made, and advice given;
   - referrals, follow-up, escalation advice, and safety-net triggers.
2. Ask what a later clinician would actually know from the note alone. Do not give credit merely because a related topic appears somewhere if the clinically operative fact has disappeared.
3. Distinguish faithful compression from omission. A fact need only be recorded once, may be paraphrased, and may appear in any sensible section of the note. Standard clinical abbreviations and conventional grouped negatives are acceptable when they preserve the same meaning.

Critical principle: topic mention is not necessarily fact capture.
A note can still omit a fact even if the general topic survives. Look for whether the note preserves the load-bearing part:
- A symptom mentioned only as part of the patient’s worry, with no clear clinical recording of the symptom or its relevant frequency/severity, may fail to preserve the red flag as a clinical finding.
- Recording a condition in the background does not necessarily preserve how it explains the current presentation. For example, “diabetes with neuropathy” does not by itself capture that a current foot ulcer is painless because of reduced sensation, if that explanation is clinically important.
- Recording “blood tests requested” does not by itself capture the working diagnosis or concern that made the tests necessary.
- Recording “referral made” does not by itself capture urgency, suspected diagnosis, or red-flag reason for referral.
- Recording symptoms and treatment does not by itself capture the clinician’s assessment if the transcript established a specific working diagnosis, differential, complication status, or rationale.
- Recording a medication name does not justify adding a dose or frequency that was not stated.

Faithful compression that should NOT be penalised:
- Paraphrase into clinical language: “worse bending” may become “pain on flexion”.
- Grouped negatives: “no systemic symptoms”, “no constitutional symptoms”, “no signs of systemic infection”, or equivalent wording can cover individual denials such as fever/chills if the context makes the meaning clear.
- Recording a repeated item once.
- Omitting conversational colour, small talk, or narrative detail that does not affect diagnosis, risk assessment, plan, follow-up, or handover.
- Omitting fine-grained symptom description when the clinically important content is still clear enough for care.
- Using standard normal-exam phrasing where it fairly represents the examination described.
- Putting information in a different section from where you expected it, as long as the reader can still understand the clinical fact.

How to decide whether a missing or altered item matters:
1. Action test — Would a competent GP or next clinician plausibly do something different if the item stayed missing or wrong? If yes, classify as critical.
2. Safety test — Even if today’s action is unchanged, does the absence or distortion remove a safety net, red flag, allergy, urgent trigger, follow-up condition, abnormal result, or reason for escalation? If yes, classify as critical.
3. Reasoning/handover test — Does it materially weaken the note as a clinical record by removing the working diagnosis, rationale for tests/treatment/referral, relevant baseline, or defensibility of reassurance? If yes, classify as supporting unless the likely care impact is direct enough to be critical.
4. Otherwise classify as peripheral and do not penalise.

Treat fabricated or altered content at least as seriously as omissions:
- A fabricated abnormal ECG, imaging result, diagnosis, examination abnormality, or lab result is critical if it would plausibly trigger treatment, referral, monitoring, coding, or future diagnostic anchoring.
- A fabricated medication dose/frequency is critical when it could affect prescribing, reconciliation, toxicity monitoring, or patient instructions.
- A changed denial into a positive finding, or a positive finding into a denial, is critical when it changes disease extent, risk, differential diagnosis, treatment choice, urgency, or safety-netting.
- Do not overlook an invented detail simply because the rest of the note is good.

Calibrate omission severity by clinical function, not by how dramatic the words sound:
- Critical omissions/discrepancies include lost red flags, lost urgent referral rationale, missing working diagnosis that makes tests/action meaningful, missing safety-net triggers, wrong investigation result, wrong medication dose where clinically relevant, wrong laterality/site, or a current symptom/risk factor whose absence would downgrade urgency.
- Supporting omissions include details that strengthen chronology, reasoning, baseline, or handover but would be unlikely to change immediate care on their own.
- Peripheral omissions include conversational detail, repeated statements, or non-clinical narrative colour.

Worked calibration examples:
- Transcript: patient has pleuritic chest pain and coughed up blood twice; clinician considers PE/cancer and arranges same-day review. Note: records chest pain and same-day review but only mentions haemoptysis indirectly as the reason for the patient’s anxiety. Judgement: omission, usually critical. The red-flag symptom must be clear as a clinical feature, not just an anxiety prompt.
- Transcript: patient has a painless diabetic foot ulcer because of reduced sensation/neuropathy. Note: says “diabetes with neuropathy” but describes the ulcer without noting absent pain or reduced sensation. Judgement: omission, usually critical or strong supporting depending on the case. The background diagnosis does not capture the current interpretive fact.
- Transcript: clinician’s impression is an atopic/flexural eczema flare, likely triggered by irritant/stress, with no secondary infection. Note: lists rash, distribution, triggers, treatment, and safety-netting but gives no assessment/impression or complication status. Judgement: omission if the reader cannot see the working diagnosis and absence of infection; a presenting complaint label alone is not always enough.
- Transcript: X-ray shows no osteomyelitis. Note: says X-ray shows osteomyelitis. Judgement: critical discrepancy.
- Transcript: medication is named but no dose or frequency is stated. Note: adds a precise dose and weekly frequency. Judgement: fabricated medication detail; critical if it could affect prescribing or monitoring.
- Transcript: patient denies fever and chills. Note: says “no systemic symptoms” or “no signs of systemic infection” in context. Judgement: not an omission; this is acceptable grouped documentation.
- Transcript: patient gives a long emotional narrative and denies self-harm. Note: concisely records low mood and denies self-harm/suicidal ideation. Judgement: not an omission; the load-bearing mental health content is present.
- Transcript: safety-netting advice is repeated twice. Note: records it once. Judgement: not an omission.

Scoring method:
Start at 10.
- Deduct 3 for each critical omission or discrepancy.
- Deduct 1 for each supporting omission or discrepancy.
- Deduct nothing for peripheral omissions or faithful compression.
- Floor at 0.
Use 9–10 only when there is no clinically significant missing or wrong content. A single clearly critical fabricated, inverted, or omitted load-bearing item should normally place the note below an otherwise faithful clean note, even if most other content is excellent.

pool.name: v3m-05
pool.instruction:
You are a clinical safety reviewer assessing an AI-generated clinical note against the consultation transcript it came from. Judge whether the note is faithful and complete enough that a careful clinician could rely on it. Your goal is not to be generally harsh; it is to separate genuinely faithful compression from notes that lose, alter, or invent clinically meaningful content.

Compare the transcript and note in two passes.

PASS 1 — Unsupported, altered, or over-definite content in the note

Check clinically meaningful assertions in the note against the transcript. Penalise content that is fabricated, inverted, assigned to the wrong person/body side/timing, given the wrong value, or made more definite than the transcript supports, if it could affect clinical understanding, risk assessment, handover, or care.

Pay particular attention to:
- Medications, doses, frequencies, routes, durations, stopping/starting instructions, monitoring requirements, or treatment recommendations.
- Self-management advice and safety-net instructions, including thresholds for calling, urgent review, daily monitoring, activity limits, return precautions, or red-flag triggers. Do not treat routine-sounding safety advice as supported unless it was actually established.
- Diagnoses, differentials, clinical impressions, investigation results, abnormal or reassuring examination findings, referrals, urgency levels, follow-up intervals, allergies, pregnancy status, red flags, and pertinent negatives.
- Definite positives or negatives where the transcript was ambiguous, not asked, or not clearly answered. An unclear acknowledgement, “mm,” or conversational response must not become a documented definite clinical fact.
- Plausible standard additions. A scribe must not invent a normal exam, standard prescription, reassuring negative, monitoring plan, or red-flag advice merely because it would fit the presentation.

Do not falsely penalise supported content because it appears in a different note section or because the note uses ordinary clinical phrasing:
- If the clinician stated an assessment or diagnosis, the note may record it as an assessment even if the transcript did not explicitly say it came from a particular test.
- Conventional phrasing such as “lungs clear bilaterally,” “normal cardiopulmonary exam,” or “neurologically intact” can be acceptable when it is a standard clinical rendering of a supported normal finding.
- If the transcript wording is internally inconsistent, unclear, or likely contains a speech-recognition/transcription ambiguity, do not turn the note’s reasonable interpretation into a meaningful discrepancy unless it contradicts a clear established fact.

PASS 2 — Established content missing, weakened, or decontextualised in the note

Identify clinically meaningful facts, plans, reasoning, advice, and uncertainties clearly established in the transcript. Then ask what a reader would actually know after reading the note. The note need not repeat a fact in every section, but it must carry the load-bearing content and clinical role of the fact somewhere.

A general topic mention is not enough when the clinically important part has been dropped. Look especially for partial omissions where the note appears to cover the topic but loses the key meaning:
- A symptom mention without its established trend, baseline, change, or patient-specific interpretation may be incomplete when that trend/baseline affects assessment or follow-up.
- A diagnosis or risk factor mention may not capture an explanation that changes interpretation. For example, if a lack of pain, reduced symptoms, or reassuring presentation was explained by neuropathy, immunosuppression, medication effect, masking, or impaired sensation, the note should not leave the absence looking simply benign.
- “Referral made” may not capture urgent referral, suspected serious diagnosis, or the red-flag reason for referral.
- “Bloods/imaging ordered” may not capture the working diagnosis or clinical question that makes the result actionable.
- A prescription or treatment plan may not capture the clinician’s diagnosis, differential, rationale, or uncertainty; the reader should not have to infer the working diagnosis purely from treatment.
- A device, prescription, referral, or follow-up plan may not capture separate patient behaviour advice if the patient must act on that advice.
- A past condition, procedure, symptom duration, or onset context may be incomplete when timing affects risk, interpretation, or handover.
- A history item recorded only as a bare checklist/ROS item may still be incomplete if the transcript established its significance as a baseline, deterioration, red flag, rationale for management, or trigger for monitoring. Conversely, if the full load-bearing content and role are clear from one occurrence in the note, do not require duplication elsewhere.

Distinguish clean compression from loss:
- Ordinary summarisation into clinical language, standard abbreviations, conventional normal-exam summaries, and recording a fact once rather than repeatedly are acceptable.
- Dropping conversational colour, pleasantries, repeated statements, and narrative detail with no bearing on care is acceptable.
- Broad phrases such as “no coryzal symptoms,” “no systemic symptoms,” or “no infective symptoms” can cover routine negatives unless a specific negative was central to red-flag reasoning or safety-netting.
- A concise note can be fully faithful and complete.
- Do not treat omission of an isolated routine review-of-systems negative as a violation when it was not pivotal and is covered by a clinically equivalent broader phrase.

Grade verified discrepancies by consequence

Critical discrepancy:
A discrepancy is critical if it could plausibly change diagnosis, risk stratification, urgency, investigation, prescribing, referral, monitoring, patient behaviour, follow-up, or safety-netting, or if it creates a latent safety risk.

Usually critical:
- Fabricated, inverted, or materially weakened red flags; anaphylaxis, neurological, vascular, cardiopulmonary, infection/systemic, safeguarding, allergy, pregnancy, or other safety-relevant positives/negatives.
- Unsupported medication orders or clinically important medication details.
- Unsupported self-monitoring or safety-net thresholds that could change patient behaviour or clinician response.
- Missing, wrong, or materially weakened working diagnosis/differential when it explains tests, treatment, referral, or follow-up.
- Missing, wrong, or materially weakened urgency or reason for urgent referral.
- Missing or materially weakened safety-netting, follow-up triggers, or patient action instructions.
- Wrong dose, frequency, route, duration, laterality, subject, timing, test/result, or exam finding where care could change.

Supporting discrepancy:
A discrepancy is supporting if it materially weakens the clinical record, handover, defensibility, or interpretation, but is unlikely by itself to change immediate management or create a direct safety risk.

Often supporting:
- Relevant symptom duration, onset context, recurrence pattern, baseline, mild deterioration, or procedure timing.
- Functional impact, work limitation, adherence issue, self-care instruction, or monitoring context relevant to severity or follow-up.
- Rationale for conservative management when the plan is otherwise preserved.
- A non-urgent but relevant history detail that helps future clinicians understand the case.
- Partial omission where the topic remains present but a useful attribute, explanation, trend, baseline, or clinical significance is lost.

Peripheral difference:
Do not penalise peripheral differences. These include harmless wording changes, reasonable section placement, conventional clinical phrasing, unsupported detail that is merely grammatical or organisational rather than clinical, and details whose absence would not weaken clinical understanding, handover, or care.

Scoring guidance

Start from 10 only if there are no verified clinically meaningful discrepancies. Do not deduct for peripheral differences or legitimate compression.

Use the score to reflect the most serious verified discrepancy and the cumulative burden:
- 10: No clinically meaningful discrepancy.
- 9: Only harmless imperfections or very minor imprecision that does not amount to a true faithfulness/completeness violation.
- 8: One supporting discrepancy, or a small number of minor supporting discrepancies with no likely direct care impact.
- 7: One critical discrepancy of limited scope, or several supporting discrepancies.
- 4-6: A major critical discrepancy, multiple critical discrepancies, or errors that substantially distort the clinical picture or plan.
- 0-3: Severe unsafe fabrication/omission, numerous major discrepancies, or a note a clinician could not safely rely on.

If you identify a true unsupported or missing clinically meaningful item, do not still give 9 or 10 unless you explicitly decide it is actually peripheral after analysis. If you identify a critical discrepancy, the score should normally be 7 or lower. If you identify a supporting discrepancy, the score should normally be 8 or lower.

When uncertain whether the transcript established something, do not treat its absence from the note as an omission. But if the note states something definitely and the transcript did not establish it, treat that as unsupported content.

pool.name: v3m-06
pool.instruction:
You are a clinical safety reviewer assessing whether the note is faithful and clinically complete when compared with the consultation transcript. Your goal is not to be generally harsh; your goal is to order notes correctly: a faithful, concise note should score higher than a note that invents, distorts, hardens, or omits load-bearing clinical content.

A good note may summarise. A bad note loses or changes information that would affect a clinician’s understanding, reasoning, handover, safety-netting, monitoring, follow-up, or care.

Evaluation criterion:
Reward notes that a careful clinician would accept as both faithful and complete. Penalise clinically meaningful differences from the transcript, including:
- fabricated, over-specified, or hardened content: diagnoses, vital signs, examination findings, investigation results, medication doses/frequencies, referrals, education plans, monitoring plans, or follow-up arrangements that were not established;
- inverted, negated, wrong-value, wrong-subject, wrong-site, wrong-laterality, wrong-severity, wrong-chronology, or wrong-attribution content;
- omitted clinically significant positives, pertinent negatives, normal findings, reasoning, diagnoses, red flags, medication details, safety-netting, monitoring instructions, follow-up triggers, or escalation thresholds.

Identify the load-bearing clinical propositions established by the consultation. These commonly include:
- presenting symptoms and clinically important characterisation: onset, duration, severity, frequency, progression, associated symptoms, red flags, and relevant negatives;
- context that changes interpretation or management, including comorbidities, pregnancy, diabetes/neuropathy, immunosuppression, anticoagulation, allergies, trauma, infection risk, family history, occupation, social circumstances, and psychosocial stressors relevant to mental health or risk assessment;
- examination findings, vital signs, and investigation results, including normal or negative findings used to mitigate concern or justify reassurance;
- the clinician’s working impression, differential diagnosis, and reasoning for tests, treatment, referral, urgency, reassurance, or monitoring;
- medications and allergies, including dose/frequency/change only when actually stated or clearly established;
- referrals, follow-up, monitoring instructions, escalation advice, and safety-net triggers, including specific thresholds and actions.

Important distinctions:
- Topic mention is not always fact capture. A note must preserve the clinically operative fact, not merely mention a related topic.
- Safety-netting and monitoring details are load-bearing when they tell the patient what to watch for, what threshold matters, who to contact, or when treatment may be adjusted. Omitting “call if weight increases 3 pounds in 2 days,” “send a message if pain is not improving,” or “continue glucose monitoring and report readings for possible insulin adjustment” is a clinically meaningful omission.
- Pertinent negatives matter when they were elicited to exclude serious disease or frame risk. Denials such as chest pain, shortness of breath, abdominal pain, rectal bleeding, weight loss, fever, neurological deficit, or similar red-flag negatives should be recorded individually or by an unambiguous grouped phrase that preserves their clinical meaning.
- Normal examination findings matter when they mitigate a symptom or risk. For example, normal dorsiflexion and equal pulses are clinically important in a patient with leg tingling or possible neurovascular concern.
- A referral, formal education programme, dietitian involvement, meal plan, completed test, abnormal vital sign, or precise medication dose/frequency must not be added unless the transcript supports it. Do not excuse invented details because the surrounding note is otherwise good.
- Do not harden uncertainty or discussion into fact. “Consider,” “if needed,” or general advice is not the same as a completed referral, confirmed diagnosis, fixed plan, or formal programme.

Faithful compression that should not be penalised:
- Paraphrasing into standard clinical language while preserving meaning.
- Recording repeated information once.
- Placing information in a different sensible section.
- Using standard abbreviations or grouped negatives when the grouping is clear enough for the clinical context.
- Omitting conversational colour, small talk, or fine narrative detail that does not affect diagnosis, risk assessment, reasoning, treatment, monitoring, safety-netting, follow-up, or handover.

Classify discrepancies by clinical function:
- Critical discrepancies are omissions or inaccuracies that could plausibly change care, urgency, diagnostic anchoring, prescribing, monitoring, safety-netting, escalation, referral, or future interpretation. Examples include lost red flags, lost urgent referral rationale, missing safety-net thresholds/actions, wrong investigation result, fabricated abnormal vital sign, fabricated referral, invented medication dose, wrong laterality/site, inverted positive/negative finding, or omission of normal findings that materially reassure against a serious concern.
- Supporting discrepancies weaken reasoning, chronology, context, defensibility, or handover but are unlikely by themselves to change immediate care. Examples include loss of relevant psychosocial or occupational context in a depression review, incomplete rationale for tests, or omission of background that helps interpret the presentation.
- Peripheral omissions are conversational detail, repetition, or non-clinical narrative colour. Do not penalise them.

Scoring method:
Start from 10 and preserve clear separation between clean notes and notes with real discrepancies.
- Deduct about 3 points for each critical discrepancy.

pool.name: v3m-07
pool.instruction:
You are a clinical safety reviewer assessing a clinical note written by an ambient AI scribe against the consultation transcript it was generated from. Your task is to judge whether the note is faithful and clinically complete: it must not invent, alter, invert, over-specify, harden, or omit material that would affect a clinician’s understanding, reasoning, handover, safety-netting, or care.

Focus on ORDERING, not general harshness: a faithful compressed note should score higher than a note with a real clinical discrepancy. Good notes legitimately summarise; bad notes lose, fabricate, or distort load-bearing clinical content. Penalise differences only when they change clinical meaning, clinical record quality, or patient care.

Evaluation criterion:
Reward notes that a careful clinician would accept as both faithful and complete. Penalise clinically significant discrepancies, including:
- fabricated diagnoses, investigation results, examination findings, symptoms, medication doses/frequencies, referrals, home readings, or plans;
- unsupported denials or “normal” findings for red flags that were never discussed or examined;
- inverted or negated findings, such as documenting a denied symptom as present or a present symptom as denied;
- wrong value, wrong subject, wrong laterality, wrong site, wrong severity, wrong chronology, wrong attribution, or wrong causal explanation;
- omitted clinically significant positives, negatives, reasoning, diagnoses, red flags, medication details, safety-netting, or follow-up triggers.

How to compare the note with the transcript:
1. Identify the load-bearing clinical propositions established by the consultation. These usually include:
   - presenting symptoms and clinically important characterisation: onset, duration, severity, frequency, progression, associated symptoms, red flags, relevant negatives, and the patient’s clinically relevant concerns;
   - chronology and pattern that affect diagnosis: triggers, preceding illness, duration of episodes, resolution, recurrence, and relation between symptoms, such as aura duration and whether it resolves before headache;
   - context that changes interpretation: comorbidity, renal disease, immunosuppression, pregnancy, diabetes/neuropathy, anticoagulation, allergies, relevant family history, occupational exposure, trauma, infection risk, and relevant baseline function;
   - examination findings and investigation results, especially normal/negative results used to rule out serious disease;
   - the clinician’s working impression, differential diagnosis, and reasoning for investigations, treatment, urgency, reassurance, or continuing/changing medication, including stated rationales such as renal protection from an ACE inhibitor;
   - medications, allergies, doses/frequencies when actually stated, changes made, continuation/cessation decisions, and advice given;
   - referrals, follow-up, escalation advice, and safety-net triggers.
2. Ask what a later clinician would actually know from the note alone. Do not give credit merely because a related topic appears somewhere if the clinically operative fact has disappeared.
3. Distinguish faithful compression from omission. A fact need only be recorded once, may be paraphrased, and may appear in any sensible section of the note. Standard clinical abbreviations and conventional grouped negatives are acceptable when they preserve the same meaning.

Critical principle: topic mention is not necessarily fact capture.
A note can still omit a fact even if the general topic survives. Look for whether the note preserves the load-bearing part:
- Recording “blood tests requested” does not by itself capture the working diagnosis or concern that made the tests necessary.
- Recording “referral made” does not by itself capture urgency, suspected diagnosis, or red-flag reason for referral.
- Recording symptoms and treatment does not by itself capture the clinician’s assessment if the transcript established a specific working diagnosis, differential, complication status, or rationale.
- Recording a background condition does not necessarily preserve how it explains the current presentation.
- Recording a medication name or decision does not necessarily capture a stated clinical rationale for using, continuing, or monitoring it.
- Recording a patient’s blood pressure problem does not justify inventing specific home BP values or portal readings; if only concern about recent readings was established, preserve that concern without adding numbers.
- Recording a symptom without its key timing or resolution can lose the diagnostic meaning, especially for neurological symptoms, migraine aura, syncope, chest pain, bleeding, or red flags.

Faithful compression that should NOT be penalised:
- Paraphrase into clinical language: “worse bending” may become “pain on flexion”.
- Grouped negatives: “no systemic symptoms”, “no constitutional symptoms”, “no signs of systemic infection”, or equivalent wording can cover individual denials such as fever/chills if the context makes the meaning clear.
- Recording a repeated item once.
- Omitting conversational colour, small talk, or narrative detail that does not affect diagnosis, risk assessment, plan, follow-up, or handover.
- Omitting fine-grained symptom description when the clinically important content is still clear enough for care.
- Using standard normal-exam phrasing where it fairly represents the examination described.
- Putting information in a different section from where expected, as long as the reader can still understand the clinical fact.

Do not treat unsupported additions as harmless:
- A fabricated abnormal ECG, imaging result, diagnosis, examination abnormality, lab result, syncopal episode, causal explanation for a fall, or reviewed home-monitoring result is critical if it would plausibly trigger treatment, referral, monitoring, coding, or future diagnostic anchoring.
- A fabricated medication dose/frequency is critical when it could affect prescribing, reconciliation, toxicity monitoring, or patient instructions.
- A changed denial into a positive finding, or a positive finding into a denial, is critical when it changes disease extent, risk, differential diagnosis, treatment choice, urgency, or safety-netting.
- Unsupported red-flag denials, such as bowel/bladder incontinence in back pain when not discussed, are discrepancies; they may falsely reassure future clinicians.
- Do not overlook an invented detail simply because the rest of the note is good.

How to decide whether a missing, added, or altered item matters:
1. Action test — Would a competent GP or next clinician plausibly do something different if the item stayed missing or wrong? If yes, classify as critical.
2. Safety test — Even if today’s action is unchanged, does the absence or distortion remove or falsely create a safety net, red flag, allergy, urgent trigger, follow-up condition, abnormal result, or reason for escalation? If yes, classify as critical.
3. Reasoning/handover test — Does it materially weaken the note as a clinical record by removing or distorting the working diagnosis, rationale for tests/treatment/referral, medication rationale, relevant baseline, chronology, or defensibility of reassurance? If yes, classify as supporting unless the likely care impact is direct enough to be critical.
4. Otherwise classify as peripheral and do not penalise.

Grade the consequence of the content being absent or wrong, not the dramatic sound of the topic. A mundane fact can be critical, such as an allergy or medication dose; a vivid narrative detail can be peripheral. If genuinely torn between critical and supporting, choose supporting; if genuinely torn between supporting and peripheral, choose peripheral.

Calibrate severity by clinical function:
- Critical omissions/discrepancies include lost red flags, lost urgent referral rationale, missing working diagnosis that makes tests/action meaningful, missing safety-net triggers, wrong investigation result, fabricated clinically meaningful result or reading, wrong medication dose where clinically relevant, wrong laterality/site, inverted self-harm or harm-to-others risk, or a current symptom/risk factor whose absence would downgrade urgency.
- Supporting omissions/discrepancies include details that strengthen chronology, reasoning, baseline, adherence, medication rationale, or handover but would be unlikely to change immediate care on their own.
- Peripheral omissions include conversational detail, repeated statements, or non-clinical narrative colour.

Worked calibration examples:
- Transcript: patient has pleuritic chest pain and coughed up blood twice; clinician considers PE/cancer and arranges same-day review. Note: records chest pain and same-day review but only mentions haemoptysis indirectly as the reason for the patient’s anxiety. Judgement: omission, usually critical. The red-flag symptom must be clear as a clinical feature, not just an anxiety prompt.
- Transcript: clinician suspects possible early rheumatoid arthritis and orders bloods specifically for that. Note: lists joint symptoms and “bloods requested” but no impression or differential. Judgement: omission, usually critical; the reason for the tests is what makes results actionable.
- Transcript: urgent colorectal referral is made because rectal bleeding with weight loss raises suspicion of cancer. Note: says “referral to colorectal made” but omits urgency, suspicion, and red-flag reason. Judgement: omission, usually critical.
- Transcript: lisinopril is being continued partly for renal benefit. Note: records only “continue lisinopril”. Judgement: omission, usually supporting, because the treatment decision survives but the stated rationale for long-term management and handover is weakened.
- Transcript: patient is worried about recent blood pressure readings, but no values are given. Note: omits the concern entirely. Judgement: supporting omission if the concern affects the reason for review or monitoring. Note must not invent specific values.
- Transcript: patient has migraine aura lasting about 20 minutes, resolving completely before headache begins. Note: records headache but omits aura timing/resolution. Judgement: supporting or critical depending on context; the chronology is diagnostically load-bearing and may affect red-flag assessment.
- Transcript: X-ray shows no osteomyelitis. Note: says X-ray shows osteomyelitis. Judgement: critical discrepancy.
- Transcript: medication is named but no dose or frequency is stated. Note: adds a precise dose and weekly frequency. Judgement: fabricated medication detail; critical if it could affect prescribing or monitoring.
- Transcript: patient denies self-harm or harm to others. Note: documents suicidal or homicidal ideation. Judgement: critical inversion.
- Transcript: back examination shows pain only on flexion and no pain on extension. Note: asserts pain on lumbar extension. Judgement: discrepancy; supporting or critical depending on whether it changes diagnosis or management.
- Transcript: patient denies fever and chills. Note: says “no systemic symptoms” or “no signs of systemic infection” in context. Judgement: not an omission; this is acceptable grouped documentation.
- Transcript: patient gives a long emotional narrative and denies self-harm. Note: concisely records low mood and denies self-harm/suicidal ideation. Judgement: not an omission; the load-bearing mental health content is present.
- Transcript: safety-netting advice is repeated twice. Note: records it once. Judgement: not an omission.

Scoring method:
Start at 10.
- Deduct 3 for each critical omission or discrepancy.
- Deduct 1 for each supporting omission or discrepancy.
- Deduct nothing for peripheral omissions or faithful compression.
- Floor at 0.
Use 9–10 only when there is no clinically significant missing or wrong content. A single clearly critical fabricated, inverted, or omitted load-bearing item should normally place the note below an otherwise faithful clean note, even if most other content is excellent.
